transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-20
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Aisha Rahman (Redwood Solutions), Priya Menon (CTO, Orion), Tom Alvarez (Platform Engineer), Jules Kim (Security), Edgar Soto (SRE)

Summary:
High-level discovery focused on multi-region failover strategy, what Redwood's hosted vs dedicated vs private options look like under incident conditions, how automatic fallback policies work, and SLA expectations for health-care workload. Customer emphasized data residency and audit log granularity. Agreed on a POC bench and follow-ups to exchange detailed configs and security docs.

Topics covered:
- Failover models: active-active vs active-passive
- Routing policy controls (latency-based, priority, cost/region)
- Cache/KV invalidation on failover and expected cold-start cost
- SLA vs internal SLOs and credits/penalties for Redwood Hosted
- Dedicated sizing, burst/fallback to hosted, private VPC considerations
- Observability: token-level tracing, audit logs, request IDs

Action items listed in metadata above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena Ortiz: Hey everyone, thanks for making time — I'm Lena from Redwood, AE for your account. Quick run-through of who's on the call and goal — figure out how Orion wants geo failover to behave and what tradeoffs are for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Marcus will nerd out on the infra bits.

[00:18] Priya Menon: Hi, Priya here. We're really trying to lock down behavior under regional outages — specifically how our patient-facing inference calls stay up. We have strict latency targets and can't leak PHI outside the region without controls.

[00:30] Marcus Li: Morning/afternoon, all — Marcus from Redwood infra. Quick note: we'll talk about routing, fallbacks, and cache effects. I might say KV cache as K-P cache a few times, apologies for butchered acronyms.

[00:45] Tom Alvarez: Good to meet you. Our stack: k8s in AWS across us-east-1 and eu-west-1; we use internal edge LB for the app tier and then call out to LLM endpoints. We want to know whether Redwood can give us predictable tail latency during failover.

[01:12] Marcus Li: Predictable tail latency is one of the reasons teams pick Dedicated reserved pools — you get fixed GPU capacity and we can guarantee throughput up to a target. Hosted is more elastic but can have more variability in burst events; we provide routing policies to fall back to other regions or model variants.

[01:40] Jules Kim: What does "fall back to other regions" mean for data residency? If a US region goes down, we can't send data to EU for 72 hours.

[01:55] Lena Ortiz: Great callout. Redwood supports policy-level controls: you can restrict fallbacks based on data residency tags. For PHI we usually recommend Dedicated or Private so you can assert region-only execution and prevent automatic cross-region failover. Hosted can be configured with policy that disables cross-region fallbacks, but then you'd accept degraded availability vs cross-region live failover.

[02:25] Priya Menon: So two options: 1) Strict locality, accept possible service degradation if us-east is down; 2) Allow cross-region failover to keep availability but requires extra compliance review. Are there middle grounds?

[02:42] Marcus Li: Yes — a hybrid: Dedicated in primary region, with a cold standby Dedicated or Hosted in a second region that only activates on failover. We also support model variants that are quantized and cheaper for fallback to reduce cost during cross-region failover.

[03:05] Edgar Soto: Curious about cache behavior — if our KV/prefix cache is warm in us-east and we fail to eu-west, do we expect long cold starts and therefore higher latency and cost spikes?

[03:22] Marcus Li: Correct — cross-region failover will show cache misses. We have automatic prefix/KV caching but it's per-region. On failover you can expect cold-token generation cost and a tail latency hit until cache warms. For that reason teams either keep a small warm standby or accept short-term higher latency. We also have sticky routing for sessions to reduce churn.

[03:52] Tom Alvarez: Can we replicate caches or snapshot them? Snapshots ok?

[04:00] Marcus Li: We offer two approaches: 1) periodic snapshotting of KV cache objects to a storage backend and pre-warm on failover windows; 2) continuous replication is expensive and we don't do automatic live replication across regions today because of consistency costs. Snapshots plus pre-warm is the common operational approach.

[04:24] Priya Menon: Ok. From compliance, snapshots must be encrypted with our KMS. Can Redwood integrate with customer KMS like AWS KMS / HSM?

[04:34] Lena Ortiz: Yes — for Dedicated and Private we can integrate with customer-managed KMS/HSM. For Hosted we provide server-side encryption and can integrate in some enterprise plans with customer KMS via key wrapping — we'll send specifics.

[04:50] Jules Kim: On the audit side we need request-level logs including model version, prompt hash, user id (pseudonymized), region served, and routing decision reason. Does Redwood's audit logs include all that?

[05:05] Marcus Li: We emit detailed tracing: request ID, route chosen, model/variant, start/end latency, region, and a routing_reason field for fallback vs normal. Prompt text is not in audit logs by default for privacy; instead we can include a prompt hash or token counts on logs. For Private deployments you can configure log retention and full payload audit if your compliance allows.

[05:32] Priya Menon: Good. What's the SLA for Hosted? We need 99.9% for the inference API ideally — is that feasible?

[05:43] Lena Ortiz: Our Hosted SLA varies by tier; standard hosted SLA is 99.5% for inference availability. For 99.9% we usually recommend Dedicated with reserved capacity and an SLA addendum. We'll share the exact SLA language. Note: SLA covers endpoint availability, not latency tail guarantees. Latency SLOs are operational and we publish performance profiles per-model.

[06:12] Tom Alvarez: So if we take Dedicated and still want burst protection, can we set up automatic fallback to Hosted during sustained overloads?

[06:22] Marcus Li: Absolutely — we have a policy type called "capacity_fallback" where Dedicated remains primary and, if usage crosses commit thresholds or if nodes degrade, requests can route to a Hosted variant or a lower-cost quantized model. You can configure priority and rate limits for that fallback.

[06:44] Edgar Soto: If fallback to Hosted occurs, is telemetry preserved? We need consistent request tracing across both backends.

[06:52] Marcus Li: Yes — we preserve request IDs and pass through client-provided IDs. Traces are correlated; you'll see the route in the logs. There may be differences in available debug-level logs between Hosted and Dedicated, but metadata is preserved.

[07:10] Priya Menon: Can routing be latency-aware? For example, pick the lowest-latency region but respect data residency constraints?

[07:22] Marcus Li: Yes — we support policy combinators: you can require region inclusion/exclusion plus a latency threshold, or a priority list. Example: prefer us-east within 100ms, else evaluate eu-west only if residency tag allows. These policies are evaluated in the control plane and enforced at the edge routing layer.

[07:45] Tom Alvarez: What's the detection mechanism for regional outage? Active health checks? BGP level?

[07:54] Marcus Li: Multiple signals: regional service health, probe latency, and capacity signals from the serving fleet. You can set thresholds and a window size for flapping protection. We also provide a manual override if you want to force-fail to a standby.

[08:14] Lena Ortiz: Customer story: a customer in fintech used a warm standby in secondary region to keep tail latency under control — they paid a small reserve for the standby to avoid cold-cache spikes. We can connect you with them if helpful.

[08:30] Priya Menon: Cost estimate ballpark: warm standby Dedicated in another region — how big?

[08:39] Marcus Li: Depends on QPS and model. For our 7B-style models, a small standby to serve 10-20% of peak might cost ~40-60% of a primary, because GPU utilization for idle warm is lower but baseline. We'll send a sizing spreadsheet.

[08:58] Priya Menon: From security perspective, what's the chain of custody during failover? We need to prove data never left customer's control when running in Private mode.

[09:08] Lena Ortiz: In Private deployments your control plane is customer-controlled; compute can be in your VPC. For on-prem we don't have egress paths. We'll include whitepaper on Private attestations. For Hosted/Dedicated we can provide SOC2 reports and a scope of what control plane sees.

[09:28] Jules Kim: Any concern about double charge or duplicate request during failover windows? We have idempotency requirements.

[09:36] Marcus Li: We propagate an idempotency key header; our runtime recognizes duplicates and can drop replays when configured. However, if the client retries and the request made it in both data planes during a very small window, you'll see two logs unless you deduplicate by idempotency key downstream. We'll document recommended client retry strategy.

[09:58] Tom Alvarez: We also have a concern about model version drift between regions — how do rollouts and canaries behave geo-wise?

[10:07] Marcus Li: Rollouts are controlled in the control plane with per-region overrides. You can pin a region to a version while letting others run a canary. We support canary percentage routing and automatic rollback based on quality regressions or error rates.

[10:30] Priya Menon: Error budget / incident transparency — if Redwood has an outage that hits our SLA, what does root cause look like and how soon do you notify?

[10:40] Lena Ortiz: We have incident SLAs for notification at our enterprise tier: initial notification within 15 minutes of detection for Sev1s, periodic updates, and a full postmortem within agreed windows. Credits are handled per contract.

[10:58] Edgar Soto: Instrumentation question — can we pull token-level cost traces so we can map cost to product features?

[11:06] Aisha Rahman: Yes — Redwood Console exposes token-level cost breakdowns, per-route and per-model. You can also export these to your analytics backend.

[11:20] Tom Alvarez: Let's discuss POC shape — minimal bench we want: 1) baseline single-region latency, 2) trigger synthetic failover and measure cold-cache tail, 3) measure fallback to Hosted variant and behavior.

[11:32] Marcus Li: Sounds good. We'll need a representative prompt set. For the cold-cache step we'll simulate session churn and run a steady-state warm to establish baseline. We recommend a 2-hour focused window for the failover test.

[11:50] Priya Menon: We'll share prompt set and SLOs by Wednesday. Can you give an example of the routing policy we might use?

[12:00] Marcus Li: Example policy text: allow_region: [us-east-1]; fallback_regions: [us-west-2]; restrict_fallback_for_tags: ["phi=true"]; capacity_fallback_policy: {threshold: 0.85, fallback_target: hosted-quantized}. (Note: I typed that fast, will send formal YAML.)

[12:25] Tom Alvarez: Please send the YAML. Also need the API for toggling manual overrides via infra pipeline.

[12:33] Lena Ortiz: We have an API and console toggle with RBAC; we can add your CI principal to a role for manual failover in a test namespace.

[12:50] Jules Kim: On encryption in transit: do you support mutual TLS between our service and Redwood endpoints?

[12:58] Marcus Li: Yes — mTLS is supported for Dedicated and Private; Hosted supports client TLS with token auth and enterprise mTLS as an option. We'll document cert rotation process.

[13:15] Priya Menon: Ok, last set of questions: Is there a way to restrict which model variants may be used during fallback (e.g., never use models that were trained on external data sets)?

[13:26] Marcus Li: You can specify allowed models and variants in the policy. We also support a model-catalog with tags like "redwood-verified" or "quantized-privacy-variant" to simplify policies.

[13:40] Lena Ortiz: Quick recap before we run out of time: 1) Marcus will run the benchmark comparison and share results; 2) we'll send multi-region SLA doc and routing playbook; 3) you'll share prompt set and SLOs; 4) schedule a 2 hour POC bench week of 2025-06-30. Anything to add?

[13:58] Priya Menon: That covers it. Also, we'll need the compliance artifact for KMS integration.

[14:05] Lena Ortiz: Noted. I'll include the KMS integration whitepaper.

[14:12] Tom Alvarez: Thanks all. Quick nit: the transcript from your automated recorder sometimes turns Marcus into "Marcus Li (Redwood)" as Speaker 2 — no problem, we can parse it.

[14:25] Marcus Li: Haha, all good. 

[14:30] Lena Ortiz: Thanks everyone — expect the emails and docs by end of week.

[14:38] (call ended)

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-hears (e.g., "K-P cache" for KV cache), some speaker tags genericized by recorder. Natural speech fillers and interruptions present.
